articles.title: Northern Ireland cancer wait times 'dangerously long', says patient
articles.summary: The Department of Health says while cancer waiting times are "not where we want them to be", work is "underway to improve performance".
articles.body:
A man who has been fighting incurable cancer for seven years has said increased times between scans and results are becoming "dangerously long" for himself and other patients.

John McClean said waiting for medical outcomes meant he was "constantly on a knife-edge". A lack of radiologists in Northern Ireland meant scans had to be sent to Australia to be analysed, leading to further delay, he said.

Campaigners, survivors and experts have gathered at Stormont to call on the executive to make a commitment to reduce the cancer death rate by 15% by 2040.

The Department of Health (DoH) said while cancer waiting times are "not where we want them to be", work is "underway to improve performance".

McClean is backing the manifesto by Cancer Research UK.

The 51-year-old Antrim man was originally diagnosed with skin cancer but later developed tumours in his brain.

The Longer Better Lives campaign - being launched at Stormont on Tuesday - says the move would prevent around 5,900 cancer deaths between now and 2040.

Among its key recommendations are the urgent tackling of NI's "unacceptably long cancer waiting times", targeted lung screening, extending the age range of the bowel screening programme to 50-74 year olds, and quicker access to tests and scans to detect cancer.

McClean underwent stereotactic radiosurgery, which is a precise form of radiotherapy that delivers a high dose of radiation to a targeted area within the brain.

He also received neurosurgery after three tumours were discovered in his brain. A fourth tumour was discovered in 2024, which required radiotherapy.

He said he was living well with cancer, but receiving quicker scan results would reduce his high level of stress.

"I'm constantly fearful... my anxiety levels are very high all the time and the waiting lists are a big part of that, because once I have a scan I am always more anxious until I get the results," he said.

"There have been times when I've got the results and it's like I relax, because I know that there's going to be a plan.

"I've been able to do my job, but the anxiety is actually what's holding me back at the minute and that makes my life, my working life, much more difficult."

McClean, who documents his story on YouTube, praised his medical team and said the blame for the state of cancer services in Northern Ireland "is Stormont's fault".

Cancer Research UK is calling on Northern Ireland's political parties to prioritise cancer services in their manifestos ahead of next May's Assembly election.

It said more cancers could be prevented through implementing the Tobacco and Vapes Act, providing better support to stop smoking and increasing the uptake of HPV vaccinations to protect against cervical cancer.

The charity has also urged the NI Executive to introduce minimum unit pricing on alcohol and restrictions on less healthy food and drink promotions.

Its Chief Executive Michelle Mitchell said waiting times for cancer care in Northern Ireland are "unacceptable".

"We really can set an ambition to save 5,900 lives by 2040 and reduce cancer deaths by 15%. We believe that's possible and we think political action and support across all the parties is necessary to make that happen."

She said there was also an economic benefit to preventing deaths as a result of cancer as fewer people would be forced to leave employment and there was "a real opportunity to turn the tide on unacceptable cancer outcomes in Northern Ireland".

In a statement, the Department of Health said it was "committed to reducing waiting times across the system and embedding long term changes that deliver better outcomes for all patients".

"However, the absence of a three-year budget makes a major transformation of the healthcare system harder to deliver, and the minister has called for more certainty on the department's budget position to help plan for the future."

In relation to scans being sent to Australia to be analysed, the department said the increased reliance on "radiology outsourcing" had been driven primarily by growing demand across radiology services.

"Ongoing difficulties in recruiting radiologists have impacted reporting capacity while CT scanning has seen demand increase by 10% annually, adding further pressure to in-house capacity. Outsourcing enables services to continue to provide opportunities for patients to receive scans," it said.

articles.title: Heatwaves and drought lead to early grape harvest
articles.summary: While many farmers count the cost of the hot, dry summer, some have benefited from the conditions.
articles.body:
While farmers across the south of England count the cost of the hot, dry summer, some growers say they have benefited from the heatwave.

Vineyards are reporting their earliest harvest on record, with the intense summer sun producing grapes that are much higher in sugar.

Simon Priestman, of Little Waddon Vineyard near Weymouth, Dorset, said his vines had "done extremely well" and anticipated an "incredibly amazing tasting wine this vintage".

Paul Girling, of Setley Ridge Vineyard in Brockenhurst, Hampshire, says his team is on track for an early end to harvest, having begun weeks earlier than usual.

Priestman, who co-owns the vineyard with his wife, Karen, said their vines had not been adversely affected by the heat.

He said: "We don't water them, we don't irrigate them.

"The grass all around has died down to brown but they are green and the grapes have done extremely well out of it.

"All of this heat and sun has put massive amount of sugars into the grapes so we are looking at very high sugar levels."

Priestman said extreme weather meant growing grapes was "a proper rollercoaster".

"I think it rained every single day of January. You can't predict what's going to happen," he said.

"One particular year, we lost 95% of the crop because of the mildew."

Girling and his wife, Hayley, bought Setley Ridge vineyard and farm shop 27 years ago.

He said: "We never started picking before the beginning of October, now we are usually finished by the end of September.

"We could have possibly started in August but 1 September has beaten our record by at least two weeks."

Despite the exceptional year, Girling says he and other small businesses are facing "relentless" pressure.

He said: "This year we've had additional tax placed on us to do with glass."

The Extended Producer Responsibility scheme requires businesses to pay towards the cost of recycling packaging used in their products, based on weight.

Girling said: "All of our glass bottles increased by 20%. Sometimes it feels like you are being taxed out of existence.

"It's just another cost we are going to have to swallow."

The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working with industry "to address pressures and make sure the scheme works well".

A spokesperson said: "These are important reforms to help our environment, already providing about £1.4bn of investment to improve our recycling system and make sure producers contribute towards the cost of managing packaging waste."

articles.title: New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani
articles.summary: The New York mayor says newly released documents show asbestos "nearly everywhere" around Ground Zero.
articles.body:
Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks, even as officials played down the health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the 170,000 documents show asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" they tested near Ground Zero, the site where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001.

"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said at a news conference with survivors.

Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the collapse of the Twin Towers have claimed more lives than the attacks themselves, US health officials say.

The document release resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued the city for the documents.

City officials found 68 boxes of the documents last year. Officials had previously said they did not have them.

"Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity," Mamadani said, standing next to television host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart. "We will do no such thing."

Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer from the terrorist attacks, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants from the building collapses.

The pages of air quality reports and other documents were released through an online portal, timed with the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

Mamdani said City Hall will spend more than $34m (£25m) on the effort. He said the documents show what the city "knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability".

More documents are to be shared over the course of the next year.

The release comes after years of survivors advocating for more transparency from city officials.

Speaking at the news conference on Tuesday, Stewart said the documents show the city didn't recognise that the air that everyone was breathing in downtown Manhattan was toxic until October of 2001.

"So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically.

The documents include an October 2001 file known as the "Harding Memo", in which an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding - serving under Mayor Rudy Giuliani - that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks.

The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)".

Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe, though research suggests people were breathing in toxic chemicals.

Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had".

Elizabeth Cascio, a former New York Fire Department (FDNY) emergency medical technician, previously told the BBC that she suffered sinus issues and headaches after responding to the attacks.

"We all knew the air quality was not safe – it was very toxic in terms of how it felt," she said. "Initially, when I came off the bus and arrived at the Trade Center, you felt like you had to hold your breath. But there's only so long you can hold your breath. I could feel the particles coming into my nose and mouth and thought: 'This can't be good'."

articles.title: One year on from Nepal protests, have Gen Z demands been met?
articles.summary: It has been a year since Nepal’s youth protested against corruption, prompting a leadership change.
articles.body:
One year ago, thousands of young people took to the streets in multiple Nepali cities to protest against corruption . Following the resulting curfews, arrests and the killing of protesters in a crackdown on the demonstrations, the Gen Z‑led movement forced the government from power, ushering in an interim administration and opening the way for new elections .

Now, as Nepal grapples with the aftermath of devastating floods along its border with Tibet, we examine what has changed over the past year – and whether the demands of the Gen Z protesters have been met.

On September 8, 2025, youth-led “Gen Z” protests began in Kathmandu and other cities of Nepal.

Demonstrators who took to the streets were protesting a series of corruption scandals in the country and were also angered by the rising trend of the children of Nepali government officials – dubbed “ Nepo kids ” – documenting their lavish lifestyles online.

The protests broke out just days after the country blocked 26 social media sites including Facebook, Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), and TikTok for not complying with government rules about “harmful” content. This ban was lifted when the protests began.

Some young demonstrators defied curfews imposed by the authorities after demonstrations began, leading to arrests and the police firing live rounds at protesters, killing about 76 people. Hundreds of protesters were injured and hundreds more arrested. Protesters also set fire to several government buildings, including parliament, and the army was deployed.

Then, on September 9, Prime Minister KP Oli, 74, resigned from his position. Within a week, Nepal’s former Chief Justice Sushila Karki had been appointed as the country’s new interim prime minister.

Ultimately, the protests culminated in the current government being formed in March this year when 35-year-old rapper-turned-politician Balendra Shah was sworn in as the country’s youngest-ever prime minister.

Shah leads the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), also known as the National Independent Party, a new anti‑establishment party which emerged after the youth-led protests and won more than two‑thirds of the 165 directly elected seats in parliament in March. Traditional parties such as the Nepali Congress and the CPN‑UML have a much smaller representation than ever before.

Although he was not a street organiser of the protests, Shah became one of the most prominent political figures, channelling Gen Z’s anger into his electoral campaign.

What were the key demands of the Gen Z protesters?

An end to corruption: Protesters demanded greater transparency and accountability from political elites they view as corrupt, as well as an end to nepotism, whereby the children of those elites live in luxury while many young Nepalis struggle financially.

Mass resignations and suspensions: Protesters called for the resignation of Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli and the mass resignation of parliamentarians. They also called for an immediate suspension of officials who issued the order to fire on protesters.

Political overhaul: The protesters called for the dissolution of parliament, establishment of an interim government and holding new general elections.

The demands have been met to some extent.

For instance, Oli resigned in the wake of the Gen Z‑led protests, and several senior members of his government also stepped down. Parliament was dissolved, an interim government was established, and new general elections were held in March this year.

“Despite the loss of life and property during the movement, the interim government successfully conducted peaceful elections, leading to the emergence of a new political force in government,” Yog Raj Lamichhane, an assistant professor at Nepal’s Pokhara University, told Al Jazeera.

“The result reflected public disenchantment with the old political establishment.”

In March this year, Nepal police arrested Oli and former Home Affairs Minister Ramesh Lekhak for their alleged involvement in the deadly crackdown on the protesters last year.

However, both men were released in April after a Supreme Court order asked the police not to indefinitely extend the detention. They remain under investigation in connection with last year’s deadly Gen Z protests, but have not been formally charged.

Furthermore, the issue of corruption among political elites has barely been addressed, observers say.

Dinesh Paudel, professor at the Appalachain State University in the US, told Al Jazeera: “The fundamental concerns and issues raised by the young protestor last year are still the same, and there are no governance style changes even after the new elected government, other than some populist rhetorics on small and cosmetic topics.”

Has the leadership change made any difference?

Some of the young leaders have entered parliament and government, while others remain in activist groups. The divisions between these two groups of people are becoming more apparent as they often clash over how much to compromise with the old political establishment.

Those who were elected to parliament in March mostly belong to the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), or National Independent Party.

“One of the most exciting and progressive parts is the emergence of youth in politics as most of the parliamentarians are young, educated and have much aspiration to change,” Bishnu Raj Upreti, a public policy analyst and research director at Nepal Centre for Contemporary Research (NCCR), told Al Jazeera.

“The leadership change appears to have brought some positive differences, particularly in the working style of the current prime minister,” Lamichhane said.

However, experts say the younger generation of MPs – those elected under the NIP/RSP banner as well as those in older parties – remains constrained by party hierarchies and Nepal’s entrenched political system.

“They are inexperienced and are still heavily controlled by party structures,” Upreti said. He added that wider generational distrust between young politicians and the older establishment also complicated reform efforts.

“Leadership change has started. It is good, but not enough.”

This has resulted in an apparent divide between those in government positions and those in activist groups.

In May this year, the new government invited Gen Z activists – mostly civil society leaders and youth activists – to give their input for constitutional amendments. However, 25 of the 29 invited boycotted the meeting, saying deeper systemic problems and earlier agreements with the previous administration were being ignored, according to Gen Z activist Aayush Basyal.

Basyal, who was present at the protests last year, said it was “really tricky” for young activists to adjust to working inside the system alongside the new Gen‑Z politicians now in office. “They are trying to cooperate with the authorities they previously challenged, while still pushing for the radical changes they demanded on the streets,” she explained.

“Now the Gen Z protesters of that time are divided into different factions, and some of the factions are vehemently opposing some work of government,” Upreti explained.

“So those who oppose the government are not in positive booking of the government,” Upreti added.

On Tuesday, families of protesters who were killed in last year’s crackdown organised a formal commemoration at what used to be Nepal’s parliament building.

After functioning as the parliament building for almost two decades, it shut down last year when Gen Z protesters trespassed and set fire to it.

Basyal said the authorities provided tight security amid rumours that some groups might try to incite violence, noting that Nepal’s “media economy” often amplifies sensational incidents even when only a few people are involved.

In the meantime, however, the divide within the Gen Z movement is becoming more stark, particularly what some see as a failure by the new leaders to advocate for protesters.

“The injured protesters have generally received medical treatment and certain monetary compensation,” Lamicchane said.

“However, the concept of compensation remains broader than financial support alone. In my view, the true compensation would be the fulfilment of the promises and objectives that inspired the Gen Z movement and the subsequent formation of a new government.”

Basyal said that while some of the people involved in the movement are now MPs or cabinet ministers, others, from poor, minority backgrounds, who lack money and influence, are still in jail and cannot speak up for themselves.

“There are people still in jail, officially more than 900 and unofficially, maybe like 1,600 plus, who are in jail for arson,” Basyal said.

He said it was troubling that these protesters remain in jail, suggesting this risks becoming “institutionalised” and raising questions over whether the government is effectively celebrating impunity.

Activists, he added, hope the new administration will treat these detainees better, but “that is yet to be seen.”

Analysts say structural changes are necessary.

“Although the government has promised reforms, particularly through changes in laws and policies, these commitments have not yet been substantially realised,” Lamichhane said.

Upreti noted that the new government has not begun any structural changes at all.

“Structural changes have to start with changing existing laws and bringing in new laws and policies,” he said.

“From what we’ve seen so far, the new leaders don’t appear to be prioritising that. Massive reform of the bureaucracy is a precondition to achieving the aims of the Gen Z movement, but the government has not yet done meaningful work in this line.”

He added that another important element is to develop better relations and deeper trust with Nepal’s two giant neighbours, India and China, since Nepal’s economic progress and geopolitical balance depend on them.

Experts also say Nepal’s highly centralised system of government is a major obstacle to deeper structural reform.

“Strong collaboration of the federal movement with provincial and local government is the necessary condition for advancing economic progress, but they ignore provincial and local government as they have no provincial and local government. It is not a good approach,” Upreti said.

“Structural changes are necessary and they come from internal power dynamics such as urban-rural divide, inherent conflict between educated elites and peasant farmers and economic and bureaucratically institutionalised corruption,” Paudel said. “It is hard to imagine that there will be any structural changes, aiming to making people’s lives better, at this stage and under current circumstances.

“In short, Nepal has missed yet another opportunity from a popular uprising that would fundamentally address Nepali peoples desire for change.”

“This new government seems to be deeply under its own weight of expectation,” Basyal said.

He explained that historically in Nepal, there’s been an “expectation gap”: people expect a lot, governments deliver little, and that gap fuels frustration.

He said that this government has “not been transparent”.

“The prime minister, he doesn’t speak a lot in the parliament. And when he did address the parliament a few times, that was pretty chaotic, as well,” Basyal added.

“If this issue remains unaddressed, it may lead to a second wave of public disenchantment.”

Lamichhane said, however, it will take time to see if the government can address the challenges it faces.

“Let’s hope and wait for changes. Now, it’s not the appropriate time to criticise the government, as Nepal has faced an apocalypse in the form of a massive flood.”

Meanwhile, flags in Nepal flew at half-mast on Monday as the country mourned the more-than-1,300 people who are known to have died in catastrophic floods which ravaged the border region with Tibet late last month. Thousands more people are still missing.

Basyal noted that Nepal’s current constitution was finalised and promulgated in September 2015, only after the devastating April and May earthquakes created urgent political pressure to end nearly a decade of deadlock.

“It feels like the nation comes together only during national disasters. So we’re really hopeful that this sense of unity that is right now will help.”

articles.title: Two ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats
articles.summary: The King's Harbour Master and Southampton Port both declined to allow migrants ashore on Sunday.
articles.body:
Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.

When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road .

Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".

The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters.

The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.

The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.

They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.

An RNLI spokesperson said: "We are working with the relevant parties to understand the decision to deny access, and we are disappointed with the nature of the communication with our crews, who voluntarily give their time to save the lives of others at sea."

The narrow peninsula at Eastney has only one road leading in and out, which demonstrators used to block coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the area.

It led to a stand-off that lasted into the early hours of Monday.

Portsmouth City Council said it was a "completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore" and brought "needless disruption" to the area.

Langstone Harbour Master Billy Johnson said the coastguard was coordinating "a search and rescue operation" and there was "no reason not to accept" the landing of the vessels at Eastney.

"The problem was managing the public order aspect that was also taking place and the geography of the area made that very challenging for the police," he said.

"This is a new thing in the Solent and the degree to which it attracted public interest and the speed at which the public reaction was mobilised was unusual and surprising.

"The way the emergency services mobilised was really effective, with the police, Border Force, coastguard, the RNLI, ambulance and fire service working completely together - all of whom were hindered by the activities of protesters."

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

ABP said it received an enquiry about landing recovered migrants.

It said in a statement: "We had to decline the enquiry as the Port did not have suitable reception facilities available.

"If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role.

"Neither was the case in this situation."

The leader of Portsmouth City Council, Steve Pitt, said: "The Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement."

In the House of Commons yesterday Dame Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Portsmouth, referred to the boat containing 120 migrants in the Solent as an "extraordinary mega dinghy".

She said: "MPs across the Solent region were scrambling for reliable information with complete radio silence from the Home Office. As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension."

Responding for the government, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said the department would "learn any lessons that we need to" following the weekend's protests.

Asked why Eastney had been chosen as the landing site, she said: "We are of course making sure we understand what exactly happened in that circumstance."

articles.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations with Kremlin worsen
articles.summary: For years, Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the EU, but the new government has dropped the pro-Kremlin stance.
articles.body:
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities.

"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details.

Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance.

The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful".

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022.

Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger".

Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules".

Hungary's next PM would pick up if Putin calls and tell him to stop Ukraine war

Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation".

Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia.

Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked.

Former Hungarian foreign intelligence deputy head András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken.

The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote.

Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind.

Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

articles.title: In 1966, a Marin County home was completed and its buyers never left; 60 years later, after one final renovation, it is on the market for the first time at $3.295 million
articles.summary: News News: A four-bedroom Kentfield house has stayed with the same owners for nearly six decades. After a major refresh, the midcentury property is finally looki.
articles.body: A four-bedroom Kentfield house has stayed with the same owners for nearly six decades. After a major refresh, the midcentury property is finally looking for a new chapter. A Marin County home that has remained with the same owners for nearly 60 years is finally on the market, and it has undergone a substantial makeover before its debut. According to Realtor.com, the four-bedroom property at 20 Hanken Drive in Kentfield was completed in 1966 and is now listed for $3.295 million. Current MLS records confirm the home was built in 1966, spans 2,784 square feet and sits on a roughly 9,600-square-foot lot. The listing describes it as being offered for the first time since it was built, making its arrival notable in a market where homes in Kentfield’s sought-after flat, established neighborhoods are rarely available in this combination of size and setting.A 1960s home with a surprisingly rare assetThe house sits in Laurel Grove on about 0.22 acres of gated, level land. Mature trees, landscaped gardens, lawns and patios surround the shingle-style exterior. That level ground is part of the property’s appeal. The home combines the privacy and greenery associated with Marin County with a layout designed for easy indoor-outdoor living.There is also a curious piece of history attached to the parcel. The property sits beside a much older home, and the original account of the listing suggests the land may have been carved out of a parcel associated with that neighboring property. That detail, however, remains an explanation from the listing agent rather than an independently established fact in the available public records.The renovation came just before the saleAlthough the house retains its midcentury character, the interiors have been extensively refreshed for its first listing. The kitchen has been remodeled with new appliances and quartzite countertops, while bathrooms have been updated. New wide-plank oak flooring and contemporary lighting were also added throughout the home.The 2,784-square-foot layout includes a living room with a fireplace and a formal dining area that lead into the remodeled kitchen. The kitchen connects to a family room, with both spaces opening toward the backyard. Upstairs, all four bedrooms are grouped together, including the primary suite, a feature the listing emphasizes as an unusual advantage of the floor plan. A two-car garage and additional storage complete the practical side of the property.There is another unusual perk for the buyerThe house also sits directly across from the Priory Tennis & Swim Club. According to the listing, the current owner has a charter membership that will transfer with the sale, allowing the new owner to bypass the club’s waitlist. The property’s location also puts residents close to Kentfield schools, local shops, restaurants and parks.For a house completed in 1966, however, its biggest selling point may be less about what has changed than what has remained: the established trees, generous outdoor space and carefully preserved sense of privacy. After nearly six decades with one set of owners, 20 Hanken Drive is now being offered at $3.295 million, giving a new buyer the rare opportunity to become only its next chapter, rather than simply another owner in a long line of them.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Putin, Trump hold 1-hour call after visit by US envoys to broker Russia-Ukraine peace
articles.summary: US News: Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump held a one-hour phone call on Tuesday, discussing the outcome of recent visits by US en.
articles.body: Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump held a one-hour phone call on Tuesday, discussing the outcome of recent visits by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv as Washington seeks to broker an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described the conversation as "constructive and frank" and said Trump stressed his desire for the war in Ukraine to end as soon as possible, Reuters reported.Ushakov said Putin briefed Trump on the situation on the battlefield and told him what the United States could do to help end the conflict. He also said Putin assured Trump that Russia had no aggressive intentions towards European countries.“In view of the speculation about Russia’s alleged hostile intentions toward European countries, it was underlined that we don’t have any aggressive plans regarding Europe,” Ushakov told reporters.The call came after Witkoff and Kushner held separate meetings with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during visits to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.According to Ushakov, Putin viewed the outcome of the US envoys' visit to Moscow positively. Zelenskyy also said the American envoys had presented some "very good, worthwhile ideas" for ending the war.“As for the peace package that Kushner spoke about and the new ideas, I’ll tell you frankly, there were indeed a couple of very good, worthwhile ideas,” Zelenskyy said in audio messages answering reporters' questions.Zelenskyy seeks meeting with TrumpZelenskyy said he hoped to meet Trump around September 20, when the UN General Assembly is due to be held in New York.He indicated that securing additional Patriot air defence systems would be among his priorities in discussions with the US president, as Ukraine seeks to counter Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks.Ukraine needs 300 Patriot missiles from partners' stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors and $2 billion for additional drones, according to UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who spoke at a meeting of countries supporting Ukraine.The European Commission also approved a 3.2 billion euro ($3.7 billion) loan for Kyiv to purchase components for Patriot air defence systems, Ukraine's Defence Ministry said.Zelenskyy said negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US could resume in the autumn, while indicating that Kyiv was prepared to seek compromises on issues including grain exports and energy.Moscow says victory is closeDespite renewed diplomatic efforts, Russia has continued to signal that it believes it can achieve its military objectives.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia remained determined to accomplish its military goals and believed "victory is very close" on the battlefield."We’re very confident in our military potential,” Peskov told reporters, while saying Moscow wanted a peaceful solution and welcomed Trump's diplomatic efforts.Ushakov said Putin had briefed Trump on Russia's plans to make further battlefield gains and achieve its military objectives.The comments come as Russian and Ukrainian forces remain locked in fighting along a roughly 1,250-kilometre front line. Western officials and analysts say Russia has struggled to make significant progress despite having a larger army.The Institute for the Study of War said Sunday that Russia's advance had slowed significantly since 2025.“Russian forces will not seize Donetsk ... until 2032 at their current rate of advance — if they can seize it at all,” the Washington-based think tank said. “The Russian rate of advance has slowed significantly across the theater since 2025, when Russia’s rate of advance had already begun to slow.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Satya Niketan building collapse: MCD crackdown begins across Delhi; 24 properties demolished, 7 sealed
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has demolished 24 properties and sealed seven illegal structures across the capital following the .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has demolished 24 properties and sealed seven illegal structures across the capital following the building collapse in south Delhi’s Satya Niketan that killed seven people.According to the MCD data, quoted by news agency PTI, the civic body stepped up its enforcement drive against unauthorised construction, carrying out demolition action against 17 properties and sealing five on Tuesday alone. It also issued nine show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, two notices for sealing and 15 demolition orders, the report said.On Monday, the MCD had demolished seven properties, sealed two and issued 26 show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, four notices for sealing and 12 demolition orders.The action follows the collapse of a five-storey building in Satya Niketan on Sunday, which killed at least seven people and injured several others. The incident brought renewed scrutiny of unauthorised construction and civic enforcement in the capital.Additionally, the MCD on Monday suspended South Zone deputy commissioner Rakesh Kumar and four engineers pending disciplinary proceedings.According to MCD officials, enforcement action has been carried out across all 12 zones, including Laxmi Nagar, Vishwas Nagar, Mukherjee Nagar, Jamia Nagar, Shaheen Bagh, Tilak Nagar, Karam Pura, Karol Bagh, Ramesh Nagar, Mansarovar Garden, Chandni Chowk and Nehru Vihar. Several of these areas have substantial student populations.The drive followed a meeting between Delhi lieutenant governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu, Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and senior government and MCD officials. Authorities were directed to conduct inspections in paying guest (PG) accommodation hubs, particularly buildings suspected of violating height and floor restrictions.Sandhu also directed the chief secretary to ensure structural audits of all buildings in PG hubs within a week.Between September 1 and 8, the MCD demolished 48 properties and sealed 15, besides issuing 90 show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, 124 notices for sealing and 66 demolition orders.From June 1 to September 8, the civic body demolished 1,007 properties and sealed 471 others. It also issued 1,551 show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, 714 notices for sealing and 753 demolition orders.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: British-Indian councillor Rishi Madlani in race to succeed Keir Starmer as Labour MP
articles.summary: UK News: Rishi Madlani, a sustainable finance expert, is vying for Labour's nomination in the upcoming Holborn and St Pancras by-election after Keir Starmer's resignation, focusing on local issues and his community experience.
articles.body: Sustainable finance professional and former Labour councillor Rishi Madlani has emerged as the only British Indian candidate seeking Labour’s nomination for the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, triggered by Keir Starmer’s resignation as the London constituency’s MP, PTI reportedMadlani, 44, has lived in the constituency for 25 years and is seeking to build his campaign around his local government experience, community work and professional background in climate action and sustainable finance.“Holborn and St Pancras have been my home for 25 years, where my politics were shaped, where my activism began and where my commitment to public service was forged,” Madlani told PTI.Starmer represented the constituency from 2015 until his resignation earlier this month. He said he was stepping down to focus on “international affairs”.Madlani has received support from Labour Indians and Labour Friends of India, which have highlighted the constituency’s links with the British Indian community.V K Krishna Menon, who served as a Labour councillor in St Pancras, became India's first High Commissioner to the UK in 1947. Labour Indians said Madlani’s candidacy reflected the continuing participation of British Indians in the Labour movement.Madlani said his decision to contest the seat was based on his political priorities and local experience, rather than his heritage alone.“I am standing because I believe I have something to offer this constituency and to the Labour movement,” he said.He said he would campaign for more affordable and social housing, stronger action on climate change and an economy that supports working people.“I know this community, I know what it means to serve residents as a councillor, I understand the pressures facing families, renters, workers and young people,” Madlani said.The constituency is expected to become a closely watched battleground. Green Party leader Zack Polanski is seeking to contest the seat, while Reform UK has faced criticism over comments concerning another Labour hopeful, former Somali refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali.Labour is expected to announce its shortlist and final candidate this week. The by-election is likely to be held in October.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Reform UK would ban full-face coverings in public areas
articles.summary: It comes after masked men gathered in Dover to protest against small boat crossings.
articles.body:
Reform UK has said it would ban face coverings in public places, including burkas and balaclavas, if it won power at the next election.

Writing in the Telegraph, party leader Nigel Farage said facial coverings were "not the British way" and undermined the trust needed for a "free and open society".

His comments come after protests over the weekend, described as spontaneous by police, when masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads in Dover.

On Monday, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said police had powers over coverings at protests but added: "When people are going about their daily business, it is absolutely fine to wear them for religious reasons, and that will continue."

In his article, Farage said he was "all for the protest" in Dover but added: "This is not the way to go about it."

Arguing for a wider ban, he wrote: "Around city centres, balaclava-clad youths tear around neighbourhoods on e-bikes and scooters, terrorising residents, making them feel unsafe in their own communities.

"We've some­how accep­ted that see­ing masked people in the streets is just part of mod­ern Bri­tain. It shouldn't be.

"Which is why Reform UK is calling for a ban on all full-face coverings in public spaces. No ifs, no buts. And yes, that includes religious ones too.

"This is not a matter of targeting one group. It's about saying that in a civilised society, people should be identifiable in pub­lic".

Labour's Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month's imprisonment, or both.

The power only only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests at the Dover demonstration and described it as a "spontaneous protest". The force has said "specific statutory requirements" needed to be met for a ban.

City centre balaclava ban to be enforced

Reform MP's burka ban call was dumb, says party chair

In a policy document, Reform said current policing powers on coverings were insufficient and that if elected it would pass legislation to authorise uniformed officers to remove items used to conceal someone's identity.

Failing to remove a face covering when asked by a police officer would be an offence, according to the document, unless the covering was worn for a work-related purpose.

Local councils England and Wales have the power to tackle anti-social behaviour through public spaces protection orders (PSPO) and on Monday, Nottingham Council said it was using an order to implement a face covering ban in the city centre

The Nottingham ban is aimed at people whom police believe are concealing their identity to commit a crime or anti-social behaviour.

It will not apply to face coverings worn for religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

Reform figures have previously expressed support for prohibiting face coverings in public, but it had not previously been adopted as the party's official position.

In February, the party's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said he "personally" supported a ban on "all face coverings in public".

Farage called for a ban on the burka and other face veils as far back as 2010, when he was a member of the European Parliament.

In 2025, he said the debate should be broader than just religious face coverings, and that a wider ban should be considered.

He said events he had attended had been targeted by masked protesters, and that he didn't believe "face coverings in public places make sense".

The burka is a veil worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body, often leaving a mesh screen to see through.

It is more concealing than the niqab, a face veil that leaves the area around the eyes clear, and hijab, a term that describes headscarves that in the West most commonly cover the head and neck but leave the face clear.

Several countries have introduced restrictions on where face coverings can be worn, including France, Denmark, Germany, Norway, Chad and Algeria.

articles.title: DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE: What AfD's big win in German state election says about 'far right' uprising in Europe
articles.summary: Europe News: Many years ago, Otto von Bismarck observed that politics was “the art of the possible”. The modern European establishment appears to have inverted the Iron Chancellor’s maxim. Politics has increasingly become the art of explaining to voters why what they want is impossible, irresponsible, xenophobic, Islamophobic, nativist or, inevitably, far right. And made it impossible to vote for the so-called far-right party that’s actually willing to admit there’s a problem.
articles.body: Jeffrey Epstein’s good buddy and consent enthusiast Noam Chomsky argued that language was a means of controlling the populace. The powers-that-be decide the terms of this universal vocabulary to shape the debate and decide what’s polite and what’s not. But so often, words get used ad nauseam that they cease to have any real meaning. Like AGI. Tech bros have been announcing the imminent arrival of AGI or Artificial Generative Intelligence with every iteration with the alacrity of your food delivery guy who says he’s just getting there but, like Godot, never arrives.The same goes for the term far right, a word used with such alacrity these days that it has ceased to have any real meaning, to the point that a right inside-forward who drifts a little too close to the touchline could be deemed far right.In Europe, parties as diverse as Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally, Geert Wilders’s PVV, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK are routinely bundled together under the overarching umbrella of the far right.AfD’s recent victory, which saw them win 39 of the 83 seats in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, led to WENA’s mainstream media bandying about their favourite term with alarmist headings to the point that a non-political observer would wonder if the Fourth Reich had risen. And, this time, the Reich gets the mandatory Disney update and will now be headed by a lesbian woman with a Sri Lankan partner.But what does the AfD actually stand for?Among its promises are to start remigration and deportation, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new wind farms, making them slightly right of Don Quixote.It also wants sanctions on Russia lifted, nuclear power revived, Swiss-style referendums introduced, dual citizenship sharply restricted and the public broadcaster reduced to a fraction of its current size.It rejects Sharia, believes in old-school family values, rejects self-identification of genders and wants Germany’s relationship with the EU rewritten.The party’s leaders are from different walks of life.Co-leader Alice Weidel is an economist and the party’s moderate face whose partner Sarah Bossard is a Sri Lankan-born film producer who was adopted by a Swiss couple. Meanwhile, Tino Chrupalla is a master painter from Saxony who is a hit with its traditional eastern German base.Another prominent leader is Björn Höcke, a former history teacher who called Berlin’s Holocaust memorial a “monument of shame” and was convicted in 2024 for using the banned Nazi slogan “Alles für Deutschland” who remains the party’s most explosive yet popular proponent.And the newest rockstar is Ulrich Siegmund, a 35-year-old who led the party to its influential win. A businessman who sells fragrances, he has a softer public image than Höcke despite being vocal on similar issues.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose Christian Democratic Union (CDU) was dealt a crushing blow, said he was “shocked”, as most mainstream politicians are wont to be when they fail to hear people’s pleas about reality.Merz added he was searching for answers as to “why far-right populism and far-right extremism were able to rise in such a rapid manner” and that his party had underestimated “fears of the population”, an analysis that really doesn’t need one to be Otto von Bismarck to make.Of course, Merz didn’t invent the “far right” label.Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz, has treated the national AfD as a suspected right-wing extremist organisation since 2021, a designation upheld by German courts. In 2025, the agency went further and classified the entire party as confirmed right-wing extremist, but that stronger designation was subsequently suspended by a Cologne court.Several state branches are deemed “right-wing extremist” but, far right itself is not a German legal category and just a broader political and journalistic epithet that has been shoved on its shelf.Currently, German parties have an understanding that can be called a ‘firewall’, a gentleman’s agreement that no party will be part of a coalition with AfD, but given that it’s almost at the halfway mark, that wall is likely to crumble very soon.But a bigger question that one ought to answer – because no academic or mainstream WENA publication will do that honestly – is: how far right are the AfD? And what exactly is the far right?So, what exactly is the far right?The terms left and right, like most other political concepts such as democracy, beheadings and bread-free diets, come from the French Revolution, when the pro-monarchy predecessors sat on the right and the anti-monarchy sat on the left.Since then, the left-right dichotomy has been extrapolated to almost every single political movement on earth. Political scientists – who have never encountered a human activity they could not chart on a scatter plot – have a modicum of an answer.The most influential modern definition comes from Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde, who distinguishes the radical right from the extreme right but puts both under far right.The radical right follows the basic principle of popular sovereignty and contests elections – like communists in India – while rejecting liberal democracy, pluralism and institutional restraints. The extreme right – like communists elsewhere in the world – rejects democracy and, like the far left, believes that armed revolution is the only solution.The populist radical right therefore has three key ingredients for its broth: nativism, authoritarianism and populism.In simple English, that means: our country, our rules; immigrants ought to assimilate and behave themselves; and that, no matter who wins the election, a corrupt elite is ruining our lives.Populism in particular – political political scientists can agree – is neither right nor left. From Bernie Sanders to Donald Trump to Hugo Chavez, anyone the mainstream press or the old establishment cannot wrap its head around is a populist.Ergo, we can surmise that the AfD, in the political scientist’s imagination, is the populist radical right. The problem is when this terminology escapes the political-science department and enters the popular lexicon of mainstream media.The Far-Right FamilyConsider the leaders of parties deemed far-right in Europe right now.Meloni is an Atlanticist – that doesn’t mean she loves extremely long essays – who has kept Italy inside the EU consensus on NATO and supports Ukraine.In France, Marine Le Pen has built a party around French nationalism that combines welfare protectionism and a strong state.In the UK, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is a gallimaufry of old-fashioned Thatcherism, tax-cutting, deregulation and a healthy disdain for Europe. In another era, he might have worked in the Ministry of Administrative Affairs.In the Netherlands, the anti-Islamist Geert Wilders is a defender of LGBT and women’s rights, perhaps because he abhors political Islam more than any of those things.Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz is an interventionist state, speaks of the erasure of Christian civilisation and of building a Hungarian political system.Yet these parties all disagree on various things, from Russia-Ukraine and economics to state intervention and religion.There are variations even within these agreements.Wilders’s objection to Islam is through the prism of Oranje liberalism, while Orbán prefers Christian civilisation. Meloni has moderated a lot in office while Le Pen has made the National Rally respectable enough for French suburbia.Farage’s Reform does not speak the same language of blood, soil and historical destiny associated with parts of continental Europe’s radical right, yet calls out the powers-that-be in the UK for bowing down to multiculturalism.Political scientists call parts of this nativism, authoritarianism and populism. Normal voters might simply call it wanting your government to remember which country it governs.The Spanner in the Works In 2019, political scientist Shafiqur Rahman wrote a piece for the Dhaka Tribune that is perhaps the most honest critique of political Islam, a piece that can be treated as the ideological sequel of a thought first expressed on the popular South Asian blog Brown Pundits, which posited: “If and when modern humanism and liberalism crashes and burns, will future historians look back and say that Islam was the rock on which it first and decisively broke?”Rahman, in his piece, took the argument further that the stubborn defence of group identity for Muslims has made “upholding group identity respectable for all groups”.He wrote: “If Muslims can be unabashedly assertive about the sanctity of their religious identity and traditions, other groups can be unapologetic about their respective identities too.”He went on to argue that Islam had “weakened liberalism by emboldening and consolidating its enemies across established democracies” that had been vanquished post-World War II.The piece ominously ended: “Abandoning universalism and embracing identitarianism is hollowing out liberalism from within. Either the principles of liberalism apply for all groups or none at all.”Seven years later, it’s hard to argue with Rahman’s prognosis, with right-wing parties knocking on the doors of electoral democracies across Europe or having already broken the door down in America.The contradiction between liberal values for different groups always existed in plain sight. For example, they expect citizens to accept LGBT values but will give a pass to other groups when it comes to it.Karl Popper had identified a version of this problem decades earlier in The Open Society and Its Enemies with his famous paradox of tolerance. Unlimited tolerance, he argued, could eventually destroy tolerance itself if a tolerant society allowed fundamentally intolerant movements to flourish unchecked. Ergo, is it inevitable that tolerating deeply illiberal religious or cultural practices will lead to liberalism digging its own grave?Liberal democracies spent decades telling groups that preserving one’s identity was desirable. At times, they did so even when those values went against basic tenets of liberal democracies like free speech or individual freedom, and chalked it up as the hallmark of a multicultural society. But this bargain became complicated when the native majority asked: why doesn’t the same principle apply to us?If Muslim identity could be protected, why was Christian identity reactionary? If minority communities could worry about cultural erasure, why was a European majority doing the same automatically nativist?The irony is that Europe’s new right has increasingly learnt to speak liberalism’s own language. Wilders, for example, is standing on the shoulders of classic liberals and arguing that Islam threatens gay rights, women’s rights, secularism and freedom of speech. The barbarians weren’t just at the gates but quoting the constitution.Like all other things, there’s obviously an OG German reference which, in this case, is by constitutional theorist Ernst-Wolfgang Böckenförde, who famously argued that the liberal state depends on conditions it cannot guarantee. Democracy requires trust, solidarity and some conception of a shared political community, but no liberal state can coerce that in its populace without ceasing to be liberal.Which leaves Europe with a rather awkward question: if assimilation is oppressive, national culture is nativist and borders are exclusionary, what precisely holds the liberal nation together? This is the fissure that parties like AfD have exploited.Missing the WoodsOne of the signs that mainstream media has no finger on the pulse of its populace is how it often refers to any rising right-wing star as the Donald Trump of said country. Viktor Orbán was called the Trump of Hungary. Farage has been called the Trump of the UK. Even though these people had been politically active when Trump was just a reality TV star. And that perhaps explains why mainstream European parties or the press are genuinely astonished whenever a right-wing party comes knocking.For years, they have ignored their own populace’s pleas about things that have gone wrong.They didn’t listen to the views of residents worried about migration, integration, crime, cultural change or whether the social contract could survive limitless demands on it. Worse, too often they treated the vocabulary of those concerns as the problem itself.Immigration became xenophobia, anxiety about Islamism became Islamophobia, national identity became nativism and opposition to progressive orthodoxies became one phobia or another. The establishment was more bothered about labels than common sense.Across the Atlantic, the Americans made the same mistake about Trump. For years, every American establishment treated Trump as an aberration rather than asking what conditions caused his rise. Instead, his supporters were deplorables, his politics a temporary fever dream, and they assumed that normal service would resume once Trump lost.But then he won again.The American establishment missed the bus and now Europe appears determined to wait at the same bus stop.Many years ago, Otto von Bismarck observed that politics was “the art of the possible”. The modern European establishment appears to have inverted the Iron Chancellor’s maxim. Politics has increasingly become the art of explaining to voters why what they want is impossible, irresponsible, xenophobic, Islamophobic, nativist or, inevitably, far right. And made it impossible to vote for the so-called far-right party that’s actually willing to admit there’s a problem.The AfD may well be far right. Parts of it undoubtedly deserve intense scrutiny. But if almost half the electorate is willing to get on that bus, standing at the stop shouting “far right” at the passengers is not politics.Bismarck called politics the art of the possible. Perhaps the mainstream ought to start by asking why the AfD suddenly looks possible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Channel Islands flights impacted by UK air traffic control issue
articles.summary: Flights to and from the Channel Islands are delayed or cancelled following a technical issue in UK.
articles.body:
Flights across the Channel Islands are facing delays after a technical issue with the UK's air traffic control systems.

Nats, which is responsible for the UK's air traffic control systems, said on X it had identified an issue with its flight processing system and that flights were still departing and airspace was open.

However, a number of arrivals from UK airports are significantly delayed.

Jersey Airport said services between the island and UK had been impacted by the issue and that passengers should check latest information with their airline. Guernsey Airport said it was also impacted and it would extend its opening hours if required.

Gatwick, which has lifeline links to both Guernsey and Jersey, said it was affected by the issue.

The disruption has caused Jersey Bulls FA Cup replay game against Burgess Hill Town FC to be postponed until at least Wednesday.

Flightradar24 reports Eurocontrol, which support European air space, expects normal air traffic levels from UK airports will resume at 21:00 BST.

articles.title: A 2000AD boyhood comic hobby turns into a specialist Mastermind subject
articles.summary: Chris Matterface from Pelsall appears on the BBC programme with his subject the 2000 AD comics.
articles.body:
A boyhood hobby has led a man to making it through to a semi-final appearance in the famous black Mastermind Chair.

Chris Matterface, 54, from Pelsall, near Walsall, appeared on the BBC programme with his specialist subject the 2000 AD comics from the 1980s and 90s.

Gaining a credible 23 points the comic enthusiast made it through to the next round, where he will have to pick a new specialist topic.

"I can't give away exactly what I'm answering questions on in the semi-final, all I'll say is that it's popular music based, but people will have to wait and see exactly what that is," he said. The semi final is due to be filmed soon, and will broadcast on BBC1 and BBCiPlayer at a future date.

The 2000 AD comics have been published every Wednesday, except over the Christmas period, since 1977 and focus primarily on science fiction stories.

"It was very much aimed at kids when it first came out in the 70s, trying to catch that wave of scifi popularity," Matterface said.

"Over the 80s it started to morph into something for a much older audience. By the time I went to university it was required reading for most students."

"There'd be nothing worse than picking something as a specialist subject, and then you go on there and you get almost all the questions wrong."

Picking a subject which has attracted hundreds of superfans meant he was aware others were comparing their answers against his while watching Monday evening's programme.

"I couldn't keep up with the notifications last night, the notification pings were going crazy on my phone, I had it upside down while the programme was on so I wanted to take it in."

articles.title: An 81-year-old Illinois homeowner faced a $17,827.96 lien after a burst-pipe insurance claim was denied; Tyler Perry offered to clear it and provide another $25,000
articles.summary: US News: Billionaire media mogul Tyler Perry has offered to pay off an $17,827.96 property lien against an 81-year-old Illinois homeowner and give her an addit.
articles.body: Billionaire media mogul Tyler Perry has offered to pay off an $17,827.96 property lien against an 81-year-old Illinois homeowner and give her an additional $25,000 in cash after her insurance company refused to pay for repairs following a burst pipe. Brenda Daurham, a resident of Markham, Illinois, was left with major damage to her home after a pipe under her kitchen sink burst on Valentine's Day. Water flooded the kitchen and spread into nearby rooms, making the house unfit to live in. After the local fire department responded to the emergency, Daurham hired Excel Fire and Water Damage Restoration Services to clean up and repair the damage. She expected her long-standing home insurance policy to cover the costs. Instead, her insurer, Allstate, rejected the claim. The decision left an $17,827.96 restoration bill unpaid for months. Excel Fire and Water Damage Restoration Services eventually placed a mechanic's lien on Daurham's home with the Cook County Clerk on August 20.An insurance denial turns into a property lienAccording to People magazine, Daurham had paid her insurance premiums to Allstate for decades before the incident. After she filed a claim following the pipe burst, Allstate denied coverage, pointing to policy exclusions for gradual wear, tear and long-term seepage. The insurer did not consider the damage a sudden event covered by the policy. Excel Fire and Water Damage Restoration Services challenged Allstate's decision, saying the incident was a sudden and accidental plumbing failure that should have been covered under the policy. As the disagreement between Allstate and the restoration company continued without a settlement, Daurham was left in the middle. She faced the possibility of further legal costs or foreclosure proceedings linked to the lien on her home. The case received wider attention after a local television report by Chicago's CBS station, CBS News Chicago. The report showed Daurham's displacement and the financial pressure caused by the unpaid restoration bill. Viewers soon shared the story on social media, tagging Tyler Perry and asking him to step in.Tyler Perry steps in with financial reliefWithin days of the broadcast, Perry responded to the public appeals. Reports from People magazine and Rolling Out said the filmmaker and actor agreed to pay the full $17,827.96 lien, removing the legal claim against Daurham's property. Perry also promised an additional $25,000 in direct financial support. The money is intended to help Daurham cover living costs and deal with the disruption caused by being unable to live in her home while repairs continue. On social media, Perry also addressed Allstate directly. He questioned the company's handling of the claim and expressed concern that an elderly customer who had paid for insurance for decades was left facing a property lien after an unexpected plumbing emergency. Allstate has not provided a detailed public explanation of the policy terms it used to deny Daurham's claim. The company has said only that the matter remains under internal review. Neither Excel Fire and Water Damage Restoration Services nor Allstate issued further official comments on the dispute over the original restoration bill. Although the disagreement between the insurer and restoration company over who should pay the original costs remains unresolved, Perry's financial support has removed the immediate legal threat to Daurham's home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map
articles.summary: Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries.
articles.body:
Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag.

Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".

Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".

Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.

His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America".

Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.

When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.

The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear.

"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk.

"I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."

Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.

His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen.

The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.

Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.

"Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

articles.title: German foreign minister warns against economic isolation after AfD win
articles.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned against economic isolation and potential consequences for businesses amid the prospect of the far-right Altern...
articles.body:
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warns against economic isolation and national solutions in response to the far-right AfD potentially taking power in Saxony-Anhalt.

EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic also cautions against countries pursuing independent economic paths in a challenging global environment.

The AfD, critical of the EU and advocating Germany leaving the eurozone, could become the first far-right extremist party to govern a German state since World War II, raising concerns about international investment and EU cohesion.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned against economic isolation and potential consequences for businesses amid the prospect of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

"I can only urgently warn against a return to national solutions," he said during a meeting with EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic on Tuesday at the Foreign Office in Berlin.

Sefcovic also warned against countries going it alone in the face of a difficult global economic environment.

The AfD, which is highly critical of the European Union and advocates Germany leaving the eurozone, is seeking to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt after its strong showing in the state election.

It could become the first party classified by German authorities as confirmed far-right extremist to take power in a German state since the end of World War II.

When asked whether he expected this to affect international willingness to invest in Germany and Saxony-Anhalt should the state be governed by the AfD, Wadephul replied: "I hope not."

He emphasized, however, that only the EU "gives us the opportunity to ensure reasonably fair conditions for our industry on the global market. And that is why any threat to the European Union must be avoided."

Anyone advocating leaving the eurozone would jeopardize cohesion within the EU and, with it, prosperity, security and freedom, he said.

articles.title: Florida sheriff's office arrests 59 sex offenders in joint operation with US Marshals
articles.summary: Operation Riverwatch saw the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service conduct over 500 compliance checks on registered sex offenders.
articles.body: A two-month crackdown on registered sex offenders and predators in one Florida city led to 59 arrests after authorities conducted more than 500 compliance checks, according to the local sheriff’s office. The Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office said its Offender Tracking Unit teamed up with the U.S. Marshals Service for "Operation Riverwatch," which ran across Jacksonville from June 15 through Aug. 14. Detectives spent more than 230 hours conducting 535 checks of registered offenders and predators, the sheriff’s office said. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AMONG 70 ARRESTED IN MISSISSIPPI CHILD EXPLOITATION CRACKDOWN: FEDS The checks led to the arrests of 59 men and women, ranging in age from 21 to 76, who authorities said violated rules they were required to follow after being released from prison or jail. "These offenders found themselves back behind bars for breaking the rules," the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post. FLORIDA-LED OPERATION RESCUES 163 CHILDREN AROUND GLOBE IN HISTORIC STATE SWEEP, HUNTS SUSPECTED PREDATORS Florida law requires registered sexual offenders and predators to follow certain registration and reporting requirements. Violations can result in felony charges and additional registration requirements, depending on the offense, the sheriff’s office said. The sheriff’s office did not say in its post which requirements each of the 59 people allegedly violated. Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff's office for more information.
